name: Solar Strategies for Multi-Unit and Tenant-Occupied Properties in LA County

mainEntity.name: How should multi-unit property owners in Los Angeles County approach solar when some units are tenant-occupied and some are owner-occupied?
mainEntity.text: How should multi-unit property owners in Los Angeles County approach solar when some units are tenant-occupied and some are owner-occupied?

acceptedAnswer.text: For duplexes, triplexes, and small apartment buildings in Los Angeles County, solar design is more complex than for single-family homes. First, clarify your goals: reducing common-area bills, lowering tenants’ costs, boosting property value, or improving resilience. You can install a system that serves only the house or common-area meter, one that feeds specific unit meters, or a combination. Options like virtual net metering or allocation agreements, where allowed, can distribute credits among multiple accounts but require careful setup. Mixed-use buildings where some units are owner-occupied and others are rentals introduce cost-sharing and fairness questions. You might size a system primarily for the owner unit and common loads while leaving tenant meters unchanged, or you may create a rent or utility-bill credit structure tied to solar output. Each approach has tax, regulatory, and administrative implications. Some incentive programs also treat multi-unit or “master-metered” buildings differently. Work with an installer experienced in multi-family projects to map meters, loads, and rate plans. Ask them to outline different metering configurations, relative costs, and pros and cons for tenant relationships. Clear documentation and transparent communication with residents are essential to avoid disputes over who pays for what and who benefits from the solar investment over time.
acceptedAnswer.description: Multi-unit owners in Los Angeles County must decide whether solar offsets common-area loads, individual unit meters, or both. For mixed tenant and owner-occupied buildings, strategies include separate systems, virtual net metering, or bill-credit arrangements, each with different complexity, cost-sharing, and regulatory implications.
